scope.flow: swap(SYNTH -> BASE) redeem-cap bypass when one synth supply is zero
scope.environment: LatentSwapLogic.sol market with aToken and zToken synthetic tokens and base asset collateral
evidence: The redeem cap, which prevent large rapid withdrawals can be completely bypassed by using swap() instead of redeem().
This is possible when the total supply of one of the market's synthetic tokens (aToken or zToken) is zero. An attacker can achieve this state through normal swaps.

Once in this state, if the attacker swaps the entire remaining supply of the other synthetic token for the base asset, the protocol's internal logic incorrectly treats this action as a "full market exit" by all liquidity providers. This special "full exit" code path intentionally skip the redeem cap check, allowing a single user to perform a massive withdrawal that would have otherwise been blocked.
The swap(SYNTH -> BASE) function should always be subject to the redeem cap, without exception.

The best method to fix this is to modify the _calcRedeem() in LatentSwapLogic.sol. The check for a "full redeem" should be made more strict to ensure it only triggers on a true, two-sided final redemption, and cannot be triggered by a single-sided swap when one token supply is zero.
although, ensure the cap-bypassing logic is only reachable when the user is redeeming the full supply of both aToken and zToken, preventing the 0 == 0 loophole.

entities.name: malicious user
evidence: This is possible when the total supply of one of the market's synthetic tokens (aToken or zToken) is zero. An attacker can achieve this state through normal swaps.

Once in this state, if the attacker swaps the entire remaining supply of the other synthetic token for the base asset, the protocol's internal logic incorrectly treats this action as a "full market exit" by all liquidity providers. This special "full exit" code path intentionally skip the redeem cap check, allowing a single user to perform a massive withdrawal that would have otherwise been blocked.

This vulnerability defeat the protocol primary defense against a bank run. A malicious user can drain a large amount of the market underlying collateral in a single block, front-running all other users. This traps the funds of the remaining liquidity providers, who are left with a depleted pool and are still subject to the now-restrictive withdrawal cap.
